questions.stem: Lysozyme in tears and saliva breaks down bacterial cell walls. What kind of barrier is this?
options: A microbiota barrier
An adaptive immune response
A chemical barrier
A physical barrier
questions.explanation: Lysozyme is an enzyme, so it is a chemical barrier that destroys bacteria before they can enter tissues. A physical barrier blocks entry mechanically, as intact skin does. Barriers act before any immune response begins.

questions.stem: Which is a physical barrier that helps a plant prevent infection?
options: Antibodies made by cells in the phloem
A thick waxy cuticle on the leaf surface
Antimicrobial compounds stored in vacuoles
Bacteria on the roots that compete with pathogens
questions.explanation: The waxy cuticle forms a physical layer that pathogens find hard to penetrate. Antimicrobial compounds are chemical barriers and root bacteria are microbiota barriers. Plants do not make antibodies, which belong to the adaptive immune response of vertebrates.

questions.stem: A patient on a long course of broad-spectrum antibiotics develops a gut infection by a harmful bacterium. Which barrier has most likely been weakened?
options: The adaptive response, because the drug destroyed the B lymphocytes
The microbiota barrier, because harmless gut bacteria were killed
The physical barrier, because the gut lining was dissolved by the drug
The chemical barrier, because stomach acid was neutralised by the drug
questions.explanation: Normal gut microbiota compete with pathogens for space and nutrients. Broad-spectrum antibiotics kill many of these harmless bacteria, leaving room for a pathogen to multiply. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on the gut lining, stomach acid or the patient's lymphocytes.

questions.stem: How do cilia and mucus in the human airways act together to prevent infection?
options: Cilia engulf trapped pathogens and digest them with lysozyme
Mucus makes antibodies and cilia carry them into the blood
Cilia release histamine and mucus carries it to infected tissue
Mucus traps particles and cilia sweep it up and away from the lungs
questions.explanation: Sticky mucus traps dust and microbes, and the beating cilia move the mucus towards the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out. Cilia are hair-like projections of cells, not phagocytes, and they move mucus out of the airways rather than into the blood.

questions.stem: Which cell releases histamine at the start of an inflammatory response?
options: Mast cell
Neutrophil
Natural killer cell
Plasma cell
questions.explanation: Mast cells in connective tissue release histamine when tissue is damaged or an allergen binds. Histamine dilates blood vessels and makes capillaries leakier. Neutrophils arrive afterwards, drawn in by chemical signals, and plasma cells belong to the adaptive response.

questions.stem: During inflammation, why does the injured area become swollen?
options: Histamine makes capillaries leakier, so fluid moves into the tissue
Histamine narrows the blood vessels, so blood is trapped in the tissue
Antibodies bind to the pathogens, so clumps of cells block the vessels
Complement proteins burst the capillaries, so blood floods the tissue
questions.explanation: Increased capillary permeability lets plasma and phagocytes move into the tissue, causing swelling; vasodilation, not narrowing, causes the redness and heat. Clumping by antibodies is agglutination, part of the adaptive response, and is not what causes the swelling of inflammation.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the main steps of an inflammatory response?
options: Vasoconstriction → histamine release → tissue repair → phagocytes arrive
Histamine release → vasodilation and leaky capillaries → phagocytes arrive → tissue repair
Phagocytes arrive → histamine release → vasodilation and leaky capillaries → tissue repair
Antibodies released → histamine release → phagocytes arrive → vasodilation
questions.explanation: Mast cells release histamine, which dilates vessels and makes capillaries leaky, so chemical signals draw phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages in to engulf pathogens, and then the tissue is repaired. Inflammation is innate, so it does not wait for antibodies.

questions.stem: Which innate immune cell is usually the first phagocyte to arrive at a site of infection and is short-lived?
options: Macrophage
Dendritic cell
Eosinophil
Neutrophil
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the most numerous white blood cells and arrive first, engulfing pathogens and dying within days; dead neutrophils are a large part of pus. Macrophages arrive later, live longer and also present antigens.

questions.stem: A person has an infection by a parasitic worm too large to be engulfed. Which innate cell is most important in attacking it?
options: Eosinophil, which releases toxic granules onto the parasite
Neutrophil, which engulfs the whole parasite by phagocytosis
Mast cell, which digests the parasite with lysozyme
Dendritic cell, which kills the parasite with perforin
questions.explanation: Eosinophils target multicellular parasites that are too large to engulf, releasing the toxic contents of their granules onto the parasite's surface. Neutrophils can only engulf small particles such as bacteria. Perforin is used by natural killer cells and cytotoxic T cells.

questions.stem: How do natural killer cells destroy virus-infected cells?
options: They engulf the whole cell and digest it in a lysosome
They secrete antibodies that bind to the viral antigens
They release histamine that makes the cell burst
They release perforin and granzymes, causing apoptosis
questions.explanation: Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes that recognise abnormal cells, such as virus-infected or cancer cells, and release perforin to make pores and granzymes to trigger apoptosis. They do not need prior exposure, unlike cytotoxic T cells. Antibodies are made only by plasma cells.

questions.stem: A cell infected by a virus releases interferons. What effect do they have?
options: The infected cell's membrane is pierced and the cell bursts
Plasma cells are triggered to make antibodies to the virus
Neighbouring cells become more resistant to viral replication
The virus particles are coated and marked for phagocytosis
questions.explanation: Interferons are signalling proteins that warn nearby cells, which then make proteins that interfere with viral replication; interferons also activate natural killer cells. Coating particles for phagocytosis is opsonisation by complement or antibodies, and piercing membranes is done by the membrane attack complex.

questions.stem: Complement proteins are activated on the surface of a bacterium. Which pair of effects can they produce?
options: Opsonising the bacterium and forming pores that lyse it
Producing interferons and presenting antigens on MHC II
Releasing histamine and forming antibodies against it
Engulfing the bacterium and presenting its antigens
questions.explanation: Complement proteins circulate in the plasma and, once activated, coat pathogens to enhance phagocytosis (opsonisation), attract phagocytes, and form a membrane attack complex that bursts bacterial cells. Histamine comes from mast cells, and engulfing pathogens and presenting their antigens on MHC II is done by antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages.

questions.stem: A dendritic cell engulfs a pathogen in the skin. What does it do next that links the innate and adaptive immune responses?
options: It stays in the skin and releases histamine to cause inflammation
It becomes a plasma cell and secretes antibodies into the lymph
It divides rapidly to form a clone of identical memory cells
It migrates to a lymph node and presents antigen to T lymphocytes
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are the main antigen-presenting cells: after engulfing a pathogen they travel through the lymphatic system to a lymph node and display antigen fragments on MHC II to helper T cells. This starts the adaptive response. Only B cells become plasma cells.

questions.stem: Which cells display MHC class II markers?
options: Only cytotoxic T cells that have been activated
Antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells
All nucleated body cells, including skin and liver cells
Red blood cells, which carry no nucleus at all
questions.explanation: MHC class II is found on antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells), which show fragments of engulfed antigens to helper T cells. MHC class I is the marker on all nucleated body cells, which is how cytotoxic T cells recognise an infected or cancerous cell.

questions.stem: Why does the immune system normally not attack the body's own cells?
options: Body cells are coated in antibodies that hide them from phagocytes
Body cells contain no proteins on the outer surface of their membrane
Lymphocytes cannot leave the blood to reach the body's tissues
Self-antigens such as MHC markers are recognised as self
questions.explanation: Each person's cells carry their own MHC markers and other self-antigens, and lymphocytes that react strongly to self are removed during development. This self-tolerance is what fails in autoimmune disease. Body cells have many surface proteins; they are recognised, not hidden.

questions.stem: Which of these pathogens is non-cellular?
options: Plasmodium, a protozoan
Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium
Candida albicans, a fungus
Influenza virus
questions.explanation: Viruses have no cells of their own; they are genetic material in a protein coat that can only replicate inside a host cell. Protozoa, bacteria and fungi are cellular pathogens. Prions, misfolded proteins, are the other non-cellular kind.

questions.stem: Pollen is harmless, yet in some people it triggers sneezing and a runny nose. What best explains this?
options: Pollen acts as an allergen, and bound IgE antibodies trigger mast cells
Pollen is a cellular pathogen that infects cells lining the nose
Pollen destroys the mucus barrier and lets bacteria enter the nose
Pollen is a self-antigen, so the body mistakes it for its own cells
questions.explanation: An allergen is a normally harmless antigen that provokes an immune response. In an allergic person, IgE antibodies bind to mast cells, and on re-exposure pollen cross-links them, triggering histamine release and inflammation. Pollen is non-self and does not infect cells.

questions.stem: A cytotoxic T cell recognises a body cell infected by a virus. What does it detect?
options: Antibodies bound to the cell's surface by a plasma cell
Histamine released from the cell's cytoplasm into the tissue
Viral antigen fragments presented on the cell's MHC class I
Viral antigen fragments presented on the cell's MHC class II
questions.explanation: Infected cells break down some viral proteins and display the fragments on MHC class I, which cytotoxic T cells recognise. MHC class II displays antigens from engulfed material on antigen-presenting cells, and is recognised by helper T cells.

questions.stem: What is the main role of lymph nodes in the immune response?
options: They are where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are made
They are where T lymphocytes mature and learn self-tolerance
They are where antibodies are broken down after an infection
They are where lymphocytes meet antigens brought in by the lymph
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes filter lymph and hold large numbers of T and B lymphocytes, so antigens and antigen-presenting cells arriving in the lymph meet the lymphocytes that can respond. Blood cells are made in the bone marrow, and T cells mature in the thymus.

questions.stem: During an infection, the lymph nodes in a person's neck become swollen and tender. What is the most likely cause?
options: Lymph has stopped flowing, so fluid has built up in the node
The pathogen is replicating inside the lymph node's fat cells
Red blood cells are collecting in the node to carry oxygen
Lymphocytes there are multiplying rapidly in clonal expansion
questions.explanation: When lymphocytes in a node recognise their antigen, they divide many times, and the node fills with dividing cells and swells. Lymph still flows through the node. Swelling is a sign of an active adaptive response nearby.

questions.stem: How does the lymphatic system act as a transport network in the immune response?
options: It carries oxygen to phagocytes so they can engulf pathogens
It carries antibodies from the lymph nodes back into the bone marrow
It carries antigens and antigen-presenting cells from tissues to lymph nodes
It carries red blood cells from bone marrow to infected tissues
questions.explanation: Lymphatic vessels collect fluid from tissues, along with any antigens and the dendritic cells that have engulfed them, and carry it through lymph nodes before returning it to the blood. Lymphocytes also move between nodes this way. Red blood cells stay in the blood vessels.

questions.stem: Which cells secrete large amounts of antibodies during an immune response?
options: Memory B cells
Cytotoxic T cells
Plasma cells
Helper T cells
questions.explanation: Activated B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies specific to the antigen. Memory B cells, from the same clone, do not secrete antibodies but persist to respond quickly if the antigen returns.

questions.stem: What is the role of helper T cells in the adaptive immune response?
options: They release cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells
They secrete antibodies that bind to pathogens in the blood
They kill infected cells by releasing perforin and granzymes
They engulf pathogens and digest them inside lysosomes
questions.explanation: Helper T cells recognise antigen on MHC II and release cytokines that stimulate the right B cells and cytotoxic T cells to divide. Killing infected cells with perforin is the job of cytotoxic T cells, and secreting antibodies is the job of plasma cells.

questions.stem: What is clonal selection in the adaptive immune response?
options: A phagocyte chooses which antigen to present to the lymphocytes
A plasma cell chooses which of its genes to make antibodies from
A lymphocyte whose receptor matches the antigen is chosen to divide
A pathogen strain that survives the immune response is chosen to spread
questions.explanation: Each B or T lymphocyte has receptors for one antigen. The antigen selects the lymphocytes whose receptors fit it, and those cells then divide into a clone; this division is clonal expansion. The selection is made by the antigen, not by a phagocyte.

questions.stem: An antibody has a Y shape. What is the role of the variable regions at the tips of its arms?
options: They are the same in every antibody so phagocytes can find them
They form antigen-binding sites specific to one epitope
They attach the antibody to the plasma cell that made it
They bind to MHC markers on the body's own cells
questions.explanation: Each antibody has two identical antigen-binding sites in its variable regions, shaped to fit a particular epitope on an antigen. The constant region, not the variable region, is the part shared by antibodies of one class and recognised by phagocytes.

questions.stem: Antibodies bind to the spike proteins of a virus, so the virus can no longer attach to host cells. What is this action called?
options: Agglutination
Opsonisation
Lysis
Neutralisation
questions.explanation: Neutralisation blocks the part of a pathogen or toxin that would bind to host cells. Agglutination is antibodies clumping pathogens together, and opsonisation is coating them so phagocytes engulf them more readily.

questions.stem: Which pairing of threat and adaptive response is most appropriate?
options: Bacteria in the blood plasma: memory T cells; virus inside a cell: neutrophils
Bacteria in the blood plasma: antibodies; virus inside a cell: cytotoxic T cells
Bacteria in the blood plasma: cytotoxic T cells; virus inside a cell: antibodies
Bacteria in the blood plasma: helper T cells; virus inside a cell: plasma cells
questions.explanation: Antibodies circulate in body fluids, so they act on extracellular threats; they cannot reach a virus once it is inside a cell. Cytotoxic T cells recognise infected cells by the antigen on their MHC I and kill them, which deals with intracellular threats.

questions.stem: A person is exposed to the same bacterium twice, six months apart. Compared with the first exposure, what happens at the second?
options: Antibody levels rise more slowly, because the first antibodies remain
Antibody levels stay the same, because the clone has already been used
No antibodies are made, because the innate response now clears it
Antibody levels rise faster and higher, because memory cells respond
questions.explanation: Memory B cells made after the first exposure persist, so the secondary response is faster and much larger, often clearing the pathogen before symptoms develop. This is the basis of active immunity and of vaccination.

questions.stem: In an experiment, mice without a thymus can still make some antibodies but cannot reject skin grafts or clear virus-infected cells. Which explanation fits best?
options: They lack complement, so infected cells are never lysed
They lack mature T cells, so cell-mediated responses fail
They lack B cells, so no plasma cells can form at all
They lack mast cells, so no inflammatory response can begin
questions.explanation: T cells mature in the thymus, so these mice have very few. Without cytotoxic T cells they cannot destroy infected or foreign cells, and without helper T cells most antibody responses are weak. B cells mature in the bone marrow, which is why some antibodies are still made.

questions.stem: A baby receives antibodies from its mother through the placenta. What type of immunity is this?
options: Artificial active immunity
Natural passive immunity
Natural active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
questions.explanation: The antibodies are made by someone else, so it is passive, and they arrive by a normal biological process, so it is natural. The protection lasts only weeks to months, because the baby makes no memory cells of its own.

questions.stem: A bushwalker bitten by a brown snake is given antivenom containing antibodies. What type of immunity does this provide?
options: Natural passive immunity, which is slow to begin but long-lasting
Natural active immunity, which is immediate and long-lasting
Artificial passive immunity, which is immediate but short-lived
Artificial active immunity, which is immediate and long-lasting
questions.explanation: Antivenom supplies ready-made antibodies by medical intervention, so the immunity is artificial and passive. It acts at once, which is what a snakebite needs, but no memory cells form, so protection fades as the antibodies are broken down.

questions.stem: Why does a vaccination give longer-lasting protection than an injection of antibodies?
options: The vaccine stops the pathogen ever entering the body again
The vaccine antibodies are replaced by the person's red blood cells
The vaccine triggers the person's own memory cells to form
The vaccine contains more antibodies than the injection does
questions.explanation: A vaccine contains antigens, not antibodies, so it triggers an active primary response that produces memory B and T cells. Injected antibodies are eventually broken down and leave no memory. Vaccination does not stop a pathogen entering; it lets the body respond quickly when it does.

questions.stem: Which example is natural active immunity?
options: A newborn is protected by antibodies from its mother's milk
A patient is given an injection of antibodies after exposure
A child recovers from chickenpox and is protected from it later
A child receives a chickenpox vaccine and is protected later
questions.explanation: Catching the disease and recovering stimulates the person's own immune response, making memory cells, so it is active, and it happens without medical intervention, so it is natural. The vaccine is artificial active, breast milk is natural passive, and the injection is artificial passive.

questions.stem: Why can new pathogens now spread around the world faster than in the past?
options: Air travel can carry infected people between continents within a day
Pathogens now mutate faster because the climate is globally connected
Vaccines now cause new pathogens to appear in vaccinated populations
Antibiotics now allow viruses to infect more than one host species
questions.explanation: In a globally connected world, an infected person can reach another continent before showing symptoms, seeding outbreaks far from the source. Vaccines contain antigens, not live replicating new pathogens, and antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.

questions.stem: A disease once rare in a country returns after vaccination rates fall. How is this described?
options: A re-emerging disease
An emerging disease
An autoimmune disease
A non-infectious disease
questions.explanation: A re-emerging disease is a known disease that becomes more common again after being controlled, for example measles returning as vaccination falls. An emerging disease is one that is newly recognised in a population or newly appears in humans.

questions.stem: A new respiratory illness appears. Health officials isolate cases, trace their contacts, and require masks in hospitals. What does this set of measures target?
options: Transmission between people by droplets and close contact
Transmission by mosquito vectors that bite at night
Transmission through contaminated food and water supplies
Transmission from mother to baby across the placenta
questions.explanation: Isolation, contact tracing and masks all reduce person-to-person spread by droplets and close contact, the usual mode for respiratory pathogens. Vector-borne diseases are controlled by measures such as removing standing water and using nets, and food-borne disease by hygiene and safe water.

questions.stem: Before control measures can be chosen for a new disease outbreak, scientists usually identify the pathogen. Which technique gives the fastest identification of an unknown virus?
options: Waiting for antibodies to appear in every patient before testing
Sequencing its genetic material and comparing it with known sequences
Growing it on nutrient agar plates and counting the colonies formed
Treating patients with antibiotics and recording who recovers
questions.explanation: Genome sequencing can identify a virus and its closest known relatives within days, and the sequence lets PCR tests be designed. Viruses cannot grow on nutrient agar because they need living host cells, and antibiotics have no action on viruses.

questions.stem: What is herd immunity?
options: Protection of non-immune people when most of a population is immune
Immunity passed from parents to all their offspring through their genes
The ability of a whole herd of animals to make the same antibodies
The immune response of a person who has been vaccinated many times
questions.explanation: When a high enough proportion of a population is immune, a pathogen cannot find enough susceptible hosts to keep spreading, so people who cannot be vaccinated are protected too. Immunity is not inherited through genes; memory cells form in each individual.

questions.stem: Why do people who cannot be vaccinated, such as some cancer patients, depend on high vaccination rates in their community?
options: Transmission chains are broken, so they are less likely to meet the pathogen
Vaccinated people pass their memory cells to them through close contact
Vaccinated people release antibodies into the air that protect others
High vaccination rates make the pathogen mutate into a harmless form
questions.explanation: When most people are immune, an infected person is unlikely to meet a susceptible one, so outbreaks die out and vulnerable people are shielded. Memory cells and antibodies stay in the person who made them; they are not passed to others.

questions.stem: Disease X spreads far more easily from person to person than disease Y. How would the vaccination coverage needed for herd immunity compare?
options: Higher coverage is needed for disease X than for disease Y
Lower coverage is needed for disease X than for disease Y
The same coverage is needed, because herd immunity is always 50%
No coverage level works for X, because it spreads too easily
questions.explanation: The more people each case infects, the larger the share of the population that must be immune to stop the chain of transmission. Highly contagious diseases such as measles need very high coverage, around 95%, while less contagious ones need lower coverage.

questions.stem: How are hybridoma cells made in the production of monoclonal antibodies?
options: By fusing a B lymphocyte with a myeloma (cancer) cell
By fusing a cytotoxic T cell with a mast cell
By fusing a macrophage with a red blood cell
By fusing two plasma cells from different people
questions.explanation: A B lymphocyte making the wanted antibody is fused with a myeloma cell, which divides indefinitely. The hybridoma combines both features, producing one specific antibody and dividing without limit. T cells, macrophages and red blood cells do not make antibodies.

questions.stem: A monoclonal antibody used to treat breast cancer binds to a receptor found in large numbers on the cancer cells. What makes it a targeted therapy?
options: It changes the DNA of the cancer cells back to normal
It makes the patient's B cells produce more antibodies
It binds only to cells displaying that specific antigen
It kills every rapidly dividing cell in the patient's body
questions.explanation: Monoclonal antibodies are identical copies of one antibody, so they bind one specific antigen, here a receptor that is abundant on the cancer cells. This marks or blocks those cells while sparing most healthy ones. Killing all rapidly dividing cells describes conventional chemotherapy.

questions.stem: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the joints. Some treatments are monoclonal antibodies that bind a cytokine which promotes inflammation. How do they help?
options: They boost the cytokine, so the immune system clears the disease faster
They make memory cells, so the patient becomes immune to the disease
They block the cytokine, so the immune attack on the joints is reduced
They destroy the joint tissue, so there is nothing left to be attacked
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease, so the aim is to damp down the immune response. A monoclonal antibody that binds an inflammatory cytokine stops it signalling, reducing inflammation and joint damage. Boosting the cytokine would make the disease worse.

questions.stem: Some cancer cells display a surface protein that switches off cytotoxic T cells. A monoclonal antibody blocks this interaction. What is the expected result?
options: The cancer cells are made to secrete antibodies against themselves
The patient becomes passively immune to all future cancers
The cancer cells lose their MHC markers and are left alone
The patient's cytotoxic T cells can attack the cancer cells again
questions.explanation: By blocking the 'off switch', the antibody releases the brake on the T cells so they recognise and kill the cancer cells. This type of immunotherapy works with the patient's own immune system. Antibodies are made by plasma cells, not cancer cells, and the protection does not extend to all cancers.
